connection: Repository interfaces, services, DI registrations, and a permanent test suite all exist from prior sessions. Test production collaborations with hand-written and library test doubles, then verify DI lifetimes.
objectives: Contrast Moq's Mock<IClockEntryRepository> (Session 29) with a real, hand-written RecordingRepository : IClockEntryRepository test double -- both implement the same interface, by two different mechanisms.
Explain why a hand-written fake and a Moq mock are both valid test doubles, and what each costs (lines of code written by hand versus a small library dependency and some indirection).

Explain the real decision-0005 finding: Program.cs registers IClockEntryRepository as Singleton but IClockEntryService, PayrollService, and IEmployeeService as Transient -- and why that mix is safe for this specific console app.
Use ServiceComposition's real AddTimeClockCore extension to observe Scoped lifetime behavior: one instance per scope, a new instance per new scope.

visuals.title: Two real ways to fake IClockEntryRepository
visuals.explanation: Mock<IClockEntryRepository>() (Session 29, via Moq) and a hand-written RecordingRepository : IClockEntryRepository (this session) both satisfy the same interface for testing purposes.

visuals.title: Both doubles work because ClockEntryService depends on the interface
visuals.explanation: Session 18/20 already established this: any class implementing IClockEntryRepository can stand in wherever the interface is expected, hand-written or Moq-generated.

visuals.title: The real, mixed lifetimes in Program.cs
visuals.explanation: AddSingleton<IClockEntryRepository, ClockEntryRepository>() shares one repository; AddTransient<IClockEntryService, ClockEntryService>() creates a new service instance on every resolution.

visuals.title: Scoped sits between Transient and Singleton
visuals.explanation: ServiceComposition's AddScoped<EntryRecorder>() gives one EntryRecorder per scope -- the same instance within one scope, a different one in the next.

preQuiz.prompt: What do Mock<IClockEntryRepository>() and RecordingRepository : IClockEntryRepository have in common as test doubles?
options: Both are objects that implement the real IClockEntryRepository interface, letting a test control GetEmployeeClockEntries/GetClockEntry/SaveClockEntry's behavior without touching the real, in-memory ClockEntryRepository
Nothing -- they are unrelated testing techniques
Both require the real database to be running
preQuiz.explanation: The mechanism differs (Moq generates an implementation at runtime; RecordingRepository is a small class written by hand), but the underlying principle -- substituting an interface implementation for testing -- is identical.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does Program.cs register IClockEntryRepository as Singleton while IClockEntryService is Transient?
options: ClockEntryRepository holds the actual state (_clockEntries) that ClockIn and Clockout both need to share across calls; ClockEntryService itself holds no state of its own, so a new instance per resolution costs nothing and shares the same underlying (Singleton) repository anyway
It is an arbitrary, unexplained inconsistency
Transient services cannot depend on Singleton services
preQuiz.explanation: decision-0005 documents this as real and verified against the actual Program.cs: the lifetime choice tracks which class actually needs shared state, not a uniform policy.

preQuiz.prompt: What does AddScoped<EntryRecorder>() guarantee within a single IServiceScope?
options: Every GetRequiredService<EntryRecorder>() call within that one scope returns the SAME EntryRecorder instance; a different scope gets a different instance
A new instance every single call, scope or not
Exactly one instance for the entire application's lifetime
preQuiz.explanation: Scoped is the real middle ground between Transient (always new) and Singleton (always the same) -- ServiceCompositionTests.cs demonstrates this directly with two different scopes.

concept.title: A test double replaces one collaborator
paragraphs: A hand-written fake is often clearest when it needs a small amount of state. A mocking library is useful when concise interaction configuration improves the test.
Both implement production interfaces created earlier; neither requires production code to know about tests.

concept.title: Test behavior before interaction details
paragraphs: Prefer the result or state the caller cares about. Verify a collaboration call only when making that call is itself part of the contract.
Over-specified mocks make harmless refactoring break tests.

concept.title: DI lifetimes describe reuse boundaries
paragraphs: Transient creates a new instance per resolution, Singleton reuses one container-wide instance, and Scoped reuses one instance inside a scope.
Tests resolve the real registrations to confirm the composition root matches those decisions.

lab.objective: Test production collaborations with hand-written and library test doubles, then verify DI lifetimes.
lab.startingCondition: Repository interfaces, services, DI registrations, and a permanent test suite all exist from prior sessions.
steps: Open tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj.
Add a ProjectReference to src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj if the reference is not already present.
Build the Domain.Tests project to verify the new project reference.
Create tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/ClockEntryServiceTests.cs.
In ClockEntryServiceTests.cs, declare a public sealed class named ClockEntryServiceTests.
Inside the test file, declare a private sealed recording fake that implements IClockEntryRepository.
In the fake, store the ClockEntry passed to the save method in a property named SavedEntry.
Implement the remaining interface members with the smallest behavior required by the service test.
Add a Fact method whose name states that a successful clock-in saves the new entry.
In that test, arrange the recording fake and construct ClockEntryService with it.
Act by calling the service clock-in method for a known employee ID.
Assert the successful outcome and assert that SavedEntry contains the same employee ID.
Create src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/ServiceRegistration.cs.
In ServiceRegistration.cs, declare a public static class named ServiceRegistration.
Add a public extension method that accepts IServiceCollection and registers the TimeClock repository and service graph.
Choose and register each Transient, Singleton, or Scoped lifetime explicitly rather than relying on an accidental default.
Open App/Program.cs and replace duplicate inline registrations with the new composition method while preserving the existing workflow.
Create tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/ServiceRegistrationTests.cs.
Add one focused test for each lifetime whose identity behavior matters: same instance where sharing is required and different instances where independence is required.
Build a ServiceProvider inside each lifetime test and create a scope when verifying Scoped behavior.
Run ClockEntryServiceTests and ServiceRegistrationTests.
Run the full solution test suite.
lab.expectedBehavior: Tests use the smallest useful double and prove the production DI composition behaves as intended.

commit: session-29: teach test doubles di lifetimes and service tests
review: The lab uses tests because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why would registering IClockEntryRepository as Transient (instead of the real Singleton) break ClockIn/Clockout's real behavior in Program.cs?
options: Each resolution would get a fresh, empty _clockEntries list -- ClockIn's saved entry would live in a different repository instance than the one Clockout later queries, so Clockout would never find it
Nothing would break -- Transient and Singleton behave identically for this class
It would cause a compile error
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly the scenario Session 20's lab explored -- Singleton is what lets ClockIn and Clockout share the same underlying state across two separate method calls.

postQuiz.prompt: When would you choose a hand-written fake like RecordingRepository over a Moq-based mock?
options: When the interface is small and the fake's behavior is simple enough that hand-writing it is clearer and has no extra library dependency -- both are legitimate choices, and this codebase genuinely uses both
Never -- Moq should always be preferred
Hand-written fakes are only valid for interfaces with one member
postQuiz.explanation: There is no universal rule -- IClockEntryRepository's real test suite uses both approaches in different tests, which is itself the honest answer: it depends on the specific test's needs.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntryService.Clockout were called from two different HTTP requests handled concurrently by the real WebApi project (Session 33), and IClockEntryRepository stayed registered as Singleton there too, what real risk would that introduce?
options: Concurrent requests could race on the same shared, mutable _clockEntries list with no synchronization -- a genuine risk this codebase's real, single-threaded console app never had to face
No risk -- Singleton services are always thread-safe automatically
The WebApi would fail to start
postQuiz.explanation: This is a real, forward-looking risk worth naming honestly: Singleton state that was safe in a single-threaded console app becomes a genuine concurrency concern once multiple requests can run in parallel.

reflections: Why does this codebase's test suite use two different test-double styles (Moq and hand-written) instead of standardizing on one?
What would you need to verify before trusting that IClockEntryRepository's real Singleton registration is still safe once the WebApi project (Session 33) starts handling concurrent requests?
Where might Scoped be a better fit than Transient or Singleton for a class this codebase doesn't have yet?
whatBreaks: Registering IClockEntryRepository as Transient instead of Singleton breaks the real ClockIn-then-Clockout sequence, because each resolution would receive an independent, empty _clockEntries list. Using Moq for every single test double, even trivially simple ones, adds a library dependency and a layer of setup-call indirection where a five-line hand-written fake like RecordingRepository would be just as clear. Assuming Singleton services are automatically safe under concurrent access ignores a real risk that becomes relevant the moment this codebase gains a multi-request host (Session 33).
summary: This codebase's real test suite uses two legitimate test-double styles side by side: Moq (Session 29's PayrollServiceTests.cs) and hand-written fakes (EntryRecorderTests.cs's RecordingRepository) -- both satisfy IClockEntryRepository, by different mechanisms. decision-0005's real, mixed Transient/Singleton registrations in Program.cs are safe specifically because only ClockEntryRepository holds shared state; ServiceComposition's Scoped example previews a third lifetime this console app never needed but Session 33's ASP.NET Core WebApi (one scope per request) will.
